passage:
Kishore sat in the corridor of the placement cell in Hyderabad, waiting his turn, when Gurleen came out of her interview looking pale. "I walked in, dropped my file, and said good evening at eleven in the morning." She laughed shakily. "After that the panel's faces never changed. Every answer felt like climbing uphill."
Kishore had seen it through the glass door: one panel member writing something within the first minute and barely looking up after.
That evening he helped her plan. "Your first thirty seconds: breathe at the door, smile, one line about why you want the job. Practise it till it's boring."
A week later, at another company, Gurleen came out grinning. "Calm start. And one of them told me my later answers changed her mind about my nervous first one."

qa.q: What did Gurleen say when she walked in?
qa.a: Good evening, at eleven in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen feel every answer was like climbing uphill?
qa.a: Gurleen felt nervous and discouraged, because the panel seemed to make up its mind in the first minute and she was fighting that first impression with every answer.

qa.q: What opening did Kishore suggest, and why does it help?
qa.a: Breathe at the door, smile and give one practised line about why she wants the job, so the first minute sets a calm tone the rest can build on.

qa.q: What does the second panel member's comment show about the interviewer's side?
qa.a: That an interviewer who stays open can let later answers change a first impression, which makes the interview fairer.

grounding: It shows a peer seeing how an interview's first minute shaped the rest, and how a calm opening and an open panel changed it.

passage: Last month I helped my club's seniors interview first-years for the photography society, and I'm still thinking about one of them. Imran came in, sat down, and before anyone spoke said, "I don't really have a portfolio." Our president's pen stopped. From then on, every answer Imran gave seemed to land flat with her, even the good ones. I'm Usha, and I only noticed because I'd been nervous in my own interview a year ago. At the end I asked Imran to show us one photo on his phone. It was a street vendor at dawn, and it was beautiful. The president looked at it for a long time and said, "I think I judged you in the first minute." Imran got in. Now I tell first-years: plan your first sentence.

Mock interview volunteer's note, Friday (Naveen, final year)
I sat on the panel for Farhan's mock interview for the bank internship. He walked in, bumped the chair, dropped his file, and his first words were, "Sorry, sorry, I'm so bad at this."
I watched the two faculty members on the panel. One stopped taking notes after that line. For the next ten minutes Farhan actually gave good answers, a clear one about budgeting for his college fest, but the panel kept asking him, "Are you sure?"
Afterwards one professor wrote "nervous, lacks confidence" as the first line of feedback. I don't think the answers after minute one got the same attention.
What I did next: I sat with Farhan and we practised just the first thirty seconds: walk in, pause, breathe, one calm sentence about himself. I also suggested to the panel that they note their first impression and then deliberately check it at the end.

qa.q: What were Farhan's first words in the mock interview?
qa.a: "Sorry, sorry, I'm so bad at this."

qa.q: How did the panel seem to feel about Farhan after his first line, and what shows it?
qa.a: The panel seemed doubtful about Farhan from the first minute; one member stopped taking notes and they kept asking "Are you sure?" even after good answers.

qa.q: Which two steps by Naveen could help next time, and why?
qa.a: Practising a calm first thirty seconds with Farhan, and asking the panel to check their first impression at the end, so both sides give the whole interview a fair chance.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading "nervous, lacks confidence" after giving good answers?
qa.a: Farhan may feel frustrated and discouraged, since his clear answer about the college fest seems to have been buried under his first nervous line.

grounding: It shows a peer seeing how the first minute of an interview shapes everything after, and helping both sides prepare a calm opening and stay open to updating.

passage:
Sunday night
Weird evening at the café. Urmila's family had set up a first meeting with a guy called Rohan, and she asked me to sit two tables away "just in case".
He was twenty minutes late. He came in sweating, phone in hand, and the first thing he said was about the traffic being "absolutely useless". I saw Urmila's face close like a shutter.
And then, honestly, he was nice. He asked about her painting, remembered the name of her college, laughed at himself about the traffic. But she kept her arms folded the whole time. She checked the time twice.
Walking home she said, "He's so negative." I said, "He was negative for one minute. The rest was actually sweet." She said, "First impressions matter, Sumit."
They do. But I think both of them lost the evening in the first minute. Rohan could have walked in calmer. Urmila could have let the next forty minutes count.
— Sumit

qa.q: How late was Rohan?
qa.a: He was twenty minutes late.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling after Rohan's first words, and what shows it?
qa.a: Urmila seemed put off and wary; her face closed like a shutter, she kept her arms folded and checked the time twice.

qa.q: What could each of them do differently at a first meeting?
qa.a: Rohan could take a moment to calm down and open warmly, and Urmila could notice her first reaction as only a guess and let the rest of the evening count too.

qa.q: How does Sumit see the evening differently from Urmila?
qa.a: Sumit, watching from two tables away, saw a nervous start followed by a sweet conversation, so to him the first minute shouldn't decide everything.

grounding: It shows a peer seeing how the first minutes of a first meeting shape everything after, and noticing that both sides could open calmly and stay open to updating.

passage: The bus from Thrissur broke down, and Elizabeth walked into the panchayat hall in Kuttanad twenty minutes late, sweaty and flustered, apologising as she tripped over a bench. Siddharth, who had come with her from the NGO, saw the elders exchange a look. From his seat by the door he watched the meeting play out: every idea she raised about the new water filters got a short "we'll see". It was as if the first minute had already given the answer. Then old Thomas chettan asked about upkeep, and Elizabeth answered in easy Malayalam with a story about her own grandmother's well. Siddharth saw two elders lean forward. On the ride home he said, "Next time we leave an hour early, and you open with the well story." Elizabeth laughed tiredly. "And they did change their minds, a little."

passage: Beatriz was wiping tables at the café in Lisbon when Daniel came in for his first date, the one he had been nervous about all week. She watched from behind the counter. He arrived early, which was good, but when his date walked in he stood up too fast and knocked his coffee into the sugar bowl. From then on, Beatriz could see it: the date checked her phone, answered in short sentences, sat back. Daniel kept apologising. Then, twenty minutes in, they found they both hated the same football team, and the date laughed properly for the first time. By the end they were leaning in. Later, while closing up, Beatriz told him, "The first two minutes nearly sank you. Next time, sit down, breathe, and say one easy thing before you do anything with your hands." Daniel grinned. "But she stayed."

qa.a: He knocked it into the sugar bowl.

qa.q: What was Beatriz thinking as she watched the date check her phone?
qa.a: Beatriz felt a pang of worry for Daniel, seeing how one clumsy first moment was colouring the date's whole reaction.

qa.q: What advice did Beatriz give, and why does it make sense?

Dear Shalini,
Something interesting happened at my cousin's matchmaking meeting on Sunday. I went along for moral support.
The young man arrived twenty minutes late because of a bus breakdown and walked in flustered, apologising, sweat on his collar. I could see my aunt's face close. After that, everything he said sounded wrong to her. He was actually warm and funny, asked good questions, and spoke kindly about his mother. But on the drive home, my aunt only talked about the lateness and the sweat.
My cousin, though, said, "I liked him once he calmed down." She's asked for a second meeting, at a café near his office, so he won't have to rush.
It made me think about first minutes. They're so heavy, and so unfair.
Nikita

I'm Jagdish, and I was on the student panel for the hostel council interviews, so I saw it from the other side of the table.
Manjula walked in, tripped on the mat and dropped her file. Papers everywhere. She went red and apologised four times. I watched the two seniors beside me exchange a look, and I felt it happen in me too: nervous, disorganised, not council material. We hadn't asked one question yet.
Then she answered. Her plan for the mess committee was the clearest of the day. But I noticed the seniors kept writing "nervous" in their margins even while she was being clear.
Afterwards I told the panel what I'd seen in myself: the first thirty seconds had nearly decided it. We re-read our notes from minute two onward. She came second.
Next week I'm helping first-years practise their openings. Walk in, breathe, one calm sentence.

Tuesday. Mahima watched Uday rehearse for his first internship interview in their shared kitchen. He started with, "Sorry, I'm really bad at interviews."
"Don't open with that," she said. "The first minute sticks. Try: Thank you for seeing me, I'm excited about this role." They practised it ten times over tea.
Thursday. Mahima waited in the cafe opposite the office. Through the glass she saw Uday walk in, straight-backed, shake hands and smile. Whatever he said first, the interviewer smiled back.
Saturday. Uday told her the rest had gone unevenly; he fumbled a coding question in the middle. "But she said my opening set a good tone, and she's giving me a second go at the coding."
Mahima laughed. "See? And if you ever fumble the start, fix it later. People can update."

qa.q: How did Uday first plan to open the interview?
qa.a: Uday started with, 'Sorry, I'm really bad at interviews.'

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling as she watched from the cafe?
qa.a: Mahima felt hopeful and a little nervous for Uday, and relieved to see the calm handshake and smile.

qa.q: What did Mahima help Uday prepare, and why?
qa.a: A calm first line, 'Thank you for seeing me, I'm excited about this role', because the first minute shapes the rest.

qa.q: How did the interviewer seem to see Uday?
qa.a: The interviewer responded warmly to the opening and gave Uday a second go at the coding, staying open to updating.

grounding: Shows a friend seeing how the first minute of an interview shapes what follows, and helping prepare a calm opening while staying open to updates.

passage:
Madhav, nervous about meeting the girl's family on Sunday? Let me tell you about my friend Salim's first meeting. I, Yusuf, went with him for support. We were twenty-two.
The first minute was a disaster. Salim spilled tea on her father's shoe. Everyone went stiff. I saw her mother's face close like a door, and I thought, well, that's finished.
But then her father laughed and said, "Now I don't have to polish it." And Salim took a breath and said calmly, "Let me start again. I'm Salim, I teach maths, and I'm very nervous." Everyone laughed. The girl, Nasreen, smiled for the first time.
I watched the whole afternoon change with that one sentence. The first minute mattered, but it wasn't the end. They've been married thirty years.
So, Madhav: breathe, one calm sentence to begin, and if you spill the tea, start again.

qa.q: What did Salim spill tea on?
qa.a: Salim spilled tea on her father's shoe.

qa.q: What did Yusuf think when the mother's face closed?
qa.a: Yusuf felt dismayed and was sure the meeting was finished after the first minute.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned the meeting around, and why?
qa.a: Salim's calm fresh start, 'Let me start again... I'm very nervous', gave everyone a new first impression after the spill.

qa.q: How might Nasreen have seen Salim after his second opening?
qa.a: Nasreen likely found him honest and endearing, which is why she smiled for the first time.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling watching a friend's first meeting, where the opening minute shaped everything until a calm restart let people update.
